qs.q: A patient is admitted for late diagnosis of acute pancreatitis, 8 days after symptom onset. Which pancreatic enzyme remains elevated for 7 to 14 days to aid this diagnosis?
o: Amylase remains elevated
Lipase remains elevated
Pepsin remains elevated
Trypsin remains elevated
qs.e: Lipase remains elevated for a longer duration (7 to 14 days) and is more specific for the pancreas than amylase, making it ideal for late diagnosis. Amylase rises quickly and clears quickly.
qs.s: Clinical Enzymology and Biomarkers — Notes: MCQs

qs.q: A patient with severe acute pancreatitis is monitored closely in the intensive care unit. Which specific laboratory finding is recognized as a poor prognostic indicator for the progression and severity of acute pancreatitis?
o: Hypocalcaemia due to fat saponification
Hyperkalaemia secondary to tissue necrosis
Hypomagnesaemia from renal wasting
Hypernatraemia caused by fluid shifts
qs.e: Hypocalcaemia serves as a poor prognostic sign in acute pancreatitis because calcium is consumed during the process of fat saponification. Serum amylase and lipase rise during an attack, but calcium levels reflect disease severity.
qs.s: Renal, Liver, Cardiac & Adrenal Function Tests: MCQs

qs.q: Which cellular event directly links duct obstruction to the early phase of autodigestion in acute pancreatitis?
o: Coalescence of zymogen granules with lysosomes within acinar cells
Immediate activation of nuclear factor kappa B (NFkB) transcription
Depolarization of the mitochondrial membrane via calcium overload
Upregulation of trypsinogen gene mutations in ductal epithelium
qs.e: Duct obstruction blocks exocytosis of zymogen granules, causing them to coalesce with lysosomes to form autophagic vacuoles where lysosomal enzymes activate digestive enzymes. This intracellular activation is a cornerstone of early autodigestion.

qs.q: A patient presents with severe epigastric pain radiating to the back. Which diagnostic criteria must be met to establish a diagnosis of acute pancreatitis?
o: Presence of at least two out of three criteria including typical pain, enzyme elevation > 3 times normal, or characteristic imaging
Presence of upper abdominal pain accompanied by serum amylase elevation of any degree
Confirmation of pancreatic necrosis on contrast-enhanced CT combined with elevated serum lipase
Typical clinical pain plus positive Cullen's or Grey-Turner's signs on physical examination
qs.e: Diagnosis requires two of the following three: typical pain, serum amylase or lipase > 3 times the upper limit of normal, or inflammation on imaging. Mild enzyme elevations alone are merely suggestive rather than diagnostic.

qs.q: Why is serum lipase preferred over serum amylase for the diagnosis of acute pancreatitis?
o: Lipase is more specific and persists longer in the serum than amylase
Lipase levels correlate directly with the severity of pancreatic necrosis
Amylase cannot be measured accurately during the first 48 hours
Amylase is exclusively produced by the pancreas, leading to false positives
qs.e: Lipase is more specific and sensitive than amylase, and it persists longer in the serum. Amylase can be falsely elevated in non-pancreatic conditions like parotitis or macroamylasaemia.

qs.q: What is the primary role of contrast-enhanced, thin-slice multi-detector CT scanning in acute pancreatitis?
o: Staging severity, distinguishing interstitial from necrotising pancreatitis, and identifying complications
Detecting small choledocholithiasis stones lodged within the common bile duct
Monitoring the daily therapeutic response of serum amylase and lipase levels
Providing the sole criterion required to initiate emergency conservative medical therapy
qs.e: Contrast-enhanced CT is the preferred imaging modality to stage severity, differentiate interstitial from necrotising disease, and detect complications like pseudocysts or necrosis. MRCP is more sensitive for choledocholithiasis.

qs.q: Which of the following drugs is specifically recognized as an etiologic association for acute pancreatitis?
o: Thiazide diuretics
Beta-blockers
Loop diuretics like spironolactone
Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs
qs.e: Thiazide diuretics, azathioprine, oestrogens, furosemide, sulfonamides, tetracyclines, valproic acid, and pentamidine are listed drug causes of acute pancreatitis. Beta-blockers and NSAIDs are not on this specific causative medication list.

qs.q: What is true regarding the utility of serum pancreatic enzyme levels in monitoring acute pancreatitis?
o: Absolute levels do not correlate with disease severity, making serial measurements unhelpful for monitoring
Serial measurements of serum lipase are essential for tracking the resolution of pancreatic necrosis
A falling serum amylase level indicates successful clearance of a biliary duct obstruction
Measuring both amylase and lipase simultaneously increases the prognostic accuracy for organ failure
qs.e: The absolute levels of amylase or lipase do not correlate with disease severity, and serial measurements are not helpful in monitoring the clinical course. Lipase is preferred initially for its specificity and persistence.

ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Acute pancreatitis is sudden inflammation of the pancreas that can range from mild self‑limited disease to life‑threatening organ failure. Diagnosis relies on characteristic pain, enzymes and imaging, while severity guides management.

sections.p: Acute pancreatitis is an abrupt inflammatory process of the pancreas that may extend to peripancreatic tissues. Diagnosis requires two of three criteria: typical abdominal pain, serum amylase or lipase ≥3 × upper limit, and imaging showing pancreatic inflammation.
b: Two of three criteria confirm the diagnosis
Serum lipase is more specific than amylase

sections.p: Severity is stratified by the Revised Atlanta Classification into mild (no organ failure, no local complications), moderately severe (transient organ failure or local complications) and severe (persistent organ failure >48 h). The BISAP score (0‑5) predicts early mortality.
b: Persistent organ failure = severe disease
BISAP ≥3 predicts >10 % mortality

sections.p: Causes are grouped as gallstones, alcohol, and other (hypertriglyceridaemia, drugs, infections, trauma, metabolic disorders). In low‑resource settings, gallstone disease and alcohol remain top, but infections such as HIV‑related opportunistic infections, hepatitis B, malaria, and herbal toxin exposure are notable.
b: Gallstones – most common worldwide
Alcohol – common in young males
Hypertriglyceridaemia >1000 mg/dL
Infections: HIV, hepatitis B, malaria, TB peritonitis
Herbal remedies containing toxic alkaloids

sections.p: Patients report sudden epigastric pain radiating to the back, often worsened by eating. Nausea, vomiting, and low‑grade fever are common. On exam, the abdomen is tender with guarding; a “sentinel loop” or colon cut‑off sign may be seen on plain X‑ray.
b: Pain radiating to back is classic
Sentinel loop on X‑ray suggests local irritation

sections.p: Laboratory and imaging confirm diagnosis, assess severity, and look for complications.

t.b: Is pancreatic enzyme markedly elevated? → ≥3 × ULN confirms pancreatic injury; normal lipase makes AP unlikely.
Is amylase elevated? → Supports diagnosis but less specific; may be normal in delayed presentation.
Are there leukocytosis, hemoconcentration, or hypocalcaemia? → Suggests systemic inflammation and poorer prognosis.
Is ALT >150 U/L? → Points to gallstone etiology; normal ALT does not exclude it.
Is there gallstone or biliary dilation? → First‑line imaging for biliary cause; if unavailable, proceed to CT when needed.
Does CT show necrosis or fluid collections? → Stages local complications; if CT unavailable, MRI or bedside ultrasound can guide.
Is TG >1000 mg/dL? → Hypertriglyceridaemia‑induced AP; treat with insulin or plasmapheresis if severe.

sections.p: Complications arise from necrosis, infection, systemic inflammatory response, and organ failure.
b: Persistent organ failure (respiratory, renal, cardiovascular)
Pancreatic necrosis → risk of infected necrosis
Acute peripancreatic fluid collections → may become pseudocyst
Hypocalcaemia from fat saponification – poor prognostic sign

sections.p: Early management focuses on fluid resuscitation, pain control, and addressing the aetiology. Monitoring for organ failure guides ICU admission.
b: Aggressive IV crystalloid (goal: urine output ≥0.5 mL/kg/h)
Analgesia with opioids (e.g., morphine) – avoid NSAIDs if renal risk
NPO initially; advance diet when pain improves
Treat cause: ERCP for biliary obstruction, stop alcohol, lower triglycerides
Antibiotics only for proven infected necrosis

sections.p: After discharge, patients need assessment for underlying cause, lifestyle counselling, and monitoring for late complications such as pseudocyst or chronic pancreatitis.
b: Ultrasound or MRCP to evaluate biliary stones after recovery
Alcohol cessation programs and lipid control
Vaccination against hepatitis B if risk present

sections.p: Conditions that mimic acute pancreatitis include perforated peptic ulcer, acute cholecystitis, myocardial infarction, and mesenteric ischemia.
b: Perforated ulcer – free air on X‑ray
Acute cholecystitis – RUQ pain, Murphy’s sign
MI – ECG changes, troponin rise

sections.p: Certain labs may be falsely normal or misleading early in the disease.
b: Serum lipase may be normal after >48 h of symptom onset
Calcium can be normal despite fat necrosis; monitor trends
ALT may be modestly raised in non‑gallstone AP

whenToSeekHelp: Severe abdominal pain with vomiting and inability to keep fluids down
Signs of organ failure: low blood pressure, rapid breathing, confusion
Persistent fever >38.5 °C or worsening abdominal distension

faq.q: Why is lipase preferred over amylase?
faq.a: Lipase stays elevated longer and is more specific for pancreatic injury.

faq.q: When is ERCP indicated in acute pancreatitis?
faq.a: When there is cholangitis or persistent biliary obstruction causing ongoing pancreatitis.

faq.q: Can antibiotics prevent infection in necrotizing pancreatitis?
faq.a: No; prophylactic antibiotics are not recommended unless infection is documented.
